prompt:
Solve the running-time recurrence below.

```formula essential
T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^2
where
T: the running time on input size n
n: the input size
In words: Four half-size calls are followed by quadratic outside work.
```

Assume bounded positive base-case costs and the usual integer rounding of fractional child sizes.

options.explanation: Correct. The critical exponent is two and quadratic outside work matches it, so the balanced case adds one logarithm.
This misses the log factor. Matching work on every level must be multiplied by the logarithmic level count.
There is no cubic total: each level is quadratic, and the number of levels is logarithmic.
This multiplies branching by the original outside work, ignoring the smaller child size. Four quadratic half-size children have exactly one parent’s outside work.

workedExample: Each half-size child has a quarter of the parent’s quadratic outside work, and there are four children. Those effects cancel, so every level contributes the same quadratic total. Logarithmically many levels give Θ(n² log n), where n is original input size.

prompt:
Solve the running-time recurrence below.

```formula essential
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log(n)
where
T: the running time on input size n
log: the base-2 logarithm
n: the input size
In words: Two half-size calls are followed by item count times its logarithm in outside work.
```

Assume bounded positive base-case costs and the usual integer rounding of fractional child sizes.

options.explanation: A logarithmic extra factor is not polynomially larger than leaf growth, so root domination does not apply.
Correct. The critical exponent is one, and outside work has one log factor. The balanced extension adds another log factor.
Each level’s work is at most linear times a logarithm, and depth is logarithmic; no quadratic factor appears.

options.text: The Master Theorem can't be applied
options.explanation: A narrower balanced-case statement without log factors would not cover this example. The stated extension with a nonnegative log exponent does cover it.

workedExample: The two children preserve total input size at each complete level. Their logarithmic factor becomes smaller gradually as the ranges shrink. Adding those declining logarithms introduces a second logarithm factor, giving Θ(n(log n)²). One logarithm is not a fixed polynomial gap, so root domination does not apply.
